title: Lab: Migrating Router on a Stick to Layer 3 Switching
summary: A hands-on lab replacing a router-on-a-stick design with a point-to-point Layer 3 link and SVIs on a multilayer switch, plus a structured walkthrough for troubleshooting broken inter-VLAN routing.

content.body:
Everything is pre-configured as it was at the end of the trunking lesson, with one change: **SW2 has been replaced with a Layer 3 (multilayer) switch**.

So right now:

- All hosts are already in the correct VLANs (10, 20 and 30).
- SW1 and SW2 are connected with a **trunk**.
- R1 and SW2 are connected using **router on a stick**.

The goal is to convert that router-on-a-stick design into **inter-VLAN routing via SVIs on SW2**, with a plain point-to-point Layer 3 link to R1 for traffic leaving the LAN.

Addressing used in this lab:

| Purpose | Address |
|---|---|
| VLAN 10 SVI | `10.0.0.62/26` |
| VLAN 20 SVI | `10.0.0.126/26` |
| VLAN 30 SVI | `10.0.0.190/26` |
| SW2 ↔ R1 link, SW2 side | `10.0.0.193/30` |
| SW2 ↔ R1 link, R1 side | `10.0.0.194/30` |

Because each SVI reuses the address R1 previously held for that VLAN, **no PC needs reconfiguring** — their default gateways are unchanged.

sections.title: Step 1 — replace ROAS with a point-to-point Layer 3 link

steps.narration: On R1, look at the current configuration. Press Enter to scroll one line, or Space to scroll one screen.
The physical interface has only default settings plus `no shutdown`; the three sub-interfaces sit beneath it.
Delete the first sub-interface.
Press the up arrow and change .10 to .20.
And once more for .30. In Packet Tracer these disappear immediately; on real IOS (or GNS3) they linger with a `deleted` status until reload.
Configure the physical interface with the new /30 address. `default interface g0/0` is not needed here because it already has default settings.
R1's end of the point-to-point link.
Now on SW2. Note this Layer 3 switch model required `switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q`, unlike the switch in the previous lab.
Reset the port to defaults. If it does not take effect the first time in Packet Tracer, issue it again.
Enter the interface and try `ip ?` — there is no `address` option, because the port is still in Layer 2 mode.
Convert it to a Layer 3 routed port. Now `ip ?` offers `address`.
SW2's end of the link.
Check the routing table — it is empty, even though a connected route should exist.
The reason: routing is not enabled yet. This is the command people forget.
Now the connected route appears. (Packet Tracer omits the local route here; real IOS shows both.)
Finally the default route pointing at R1.

sections.title: Step 2 — configure the SVIs and test

steps.narration: First confirm the VLANs exist — an SVI will not go up/up if its VLAN is missing. VLANs 10, 20 and 30 are present.
Create the VLAN 10 SVI.
Assign the last usable address of the subnet — the same address R1 used, so PCs keep working.
VLAN 20 SVI.
Its gateway address.
VLAN 30 SVI.
Its gateway address.
All three SVIs show up/up. Inter-VLAN routing should now work.
From PC7 in VLAN 10, ping PC3 in VLAN 30. The first ping or two may fail while PC7 ARPs for its default gateway — that is normal.
Switch to simulation mode and repeat: the traffic goes PC7 → SW2 → SW1, never touching R1. SW2 routed it from the VLAN 10 SVI to the VLAN 30 SVI internally.
Finally test the default route by pinging the Internet. Static routes on R1 and the Internet router are already in place.

content.body: The first one or two pings failing is not a fault. The PC must ARP for the MAC address of its default gateway before it can send the first packet, and the ARP exchange takes longer than the ICMP timeout.

The second half of the lab is a troubleshooting exercise: PC3 cannot ping anything, not even hosts in its own VLAN 10.

**Common causes of inter-VLAN routing problems on Layer 2 switches**

- A host is in the **wrong VLAN** — the access port is assigned to a different VLAN than the documentation says.
- The link between switches is **not a trunk** — someone forgot `switchport mode trunk`.
- The required VLAN is **not allowed** on the trunk, so that VLAN's traffic cannot pass between switches.
- A **native VLAN mismatch** between the two ends of the trunk.
- On the host side, a **wrong subnet mask** or wrong default gateway.

**How the fault was isolated**

1. PC3's `ipconfig /all` showed the right IP address and gateway but a **/24 mask instead of /25**. Fixing it did not restore connectivity — so there was a second fault.
2. PC3 could not ping **either** router sub-interface; PC1, in the same VLAN but on the other switch, could ping **both**. That pointed the finger at SW2 or the trunk between the switches, not at the router.
3. `show vlan brief` on SW1 was fine. On SW2 it showed **no ports in VLAN 10** — Fa0/3 and Fa0/4 were both in VLAN 12.
4. `show interfaces fa0/3 switchport` confirmed the port was in **static access** mode, so `switchport access vlan 10` was the fix.
5. `show interfaces trunk` on both switches showed matching native VLANs and allowed VLANs, ruling the trunk out.

After fixing PC3's VLAN, PC3 reached its gateway and PC1. A remaining fault stopped PC2 (VLAN 12) reaching its gateway while still reaching PC4 in the same VLAN — the classic signature of a problem on the **router's** sub-interface rather than in the Layer 2 path.

rows: Which VLANs exist and which access ports are in each. Trunk ports do NOT appear here
Trunk ports, mode, encapsulation, native VLAN, allowed VLANs, active VLANs
Administrative and operational mode of a single port — e.g. `static access`
IP addresses and up/up status of physical interfaces, sub-interfaces and SVIs
Per-port status, and shows `routed` in the VLAN column for routed ports
The switch's own routing table — empty until `ip routing` is enabled
Host IP, mask and default gateway — a wrong mask is a very common fault

content.body: When one host in a VLAN works and another in the same VLAN does not, the fault is local to the broken host or its switch port. When every host in a VLAN can reach each other but none can reach the gateway, suspect the router sub-interface, the SVI, or the trunk carrying that VLAN.

sections.title: Command reference: the inter-VLAN routing lab

commands.example:
R1(config)# no interface g0/0.10
R1(config)# no interface g0/0.20
R1(config)# no interface g0/0.30
commands.description: Removes the old router-on-a-stick sub-interfaces before migrating inter-VLAN routing onto the Layer 3 switch.
Configures the router end of the /30 point-to-point link to the Layer 3 switch.
commands.note: A /30 gives exactly two usable addresses — perfect for a link between two devices.

commands.description: Clears the switch port back to defaults before turning it into a routed link.
commands.note: In Packet Tracer you may need to issue this twice.

commands.description: Turns the port into a Layer 3 routed port so it can hold the other end of the /30.
Enables routing on the multilayer switch — required before it will route between the SVIs.
commands.note: Check with do show ip route: before this command the routing table is essentially empty.

commands.example:
SW2(config)# interface vlan 10
SW2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.0.62 255.255.255.192
commands.description: Creates the SVI that acts as the default gateway for each VLAN. In this lab: VLAN 10 = 10.0.0.62/26, VLAN 20 = 10.0.0.126/26, VLAN 30 = 10.0.0.190/26.
Points everything the switch does not know about at the router, so external traffic leaves the site correctly.
Confirms the VLANs exist and which access ports are in them.

commands.example:
SW1# show interfaces fa0/3 switchport
Administrative Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 10
commands.description: Shows the full Layer 2 configuration of a port: its administrative and operational mode, access VLAN, trunk settings and native VLAN.
Confirms the switch-to-switch links are trunking and carrying the required VLANs.
Confirms the SVIs and the routed port are up/up with the right addresses.
End-to-end test. Pinging between VLANs proves inter-VLAN routing works; pinging an external address proves the default route works.
commands.note: The first ping may time out while ARP resolves — send it twice before concluding something is broken.

commands.description: Shows the PC's IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and MAC address — the first thing to check when a host cannot reach other VLANs.

questions.question: You configure `no switchport` and an IP address on a Layer 3 switch port, but `show ip route` shows no routes at all. What is missing?
questions.explanation: The switch will not build a routing table until `ip routing` is enabled globally. Without it, even connected routes for routed ports do not appear.

options.label: A
options.text: `ip routing` has not been enabled globally

options.label: B
options.text: The port needs `switchport mode trunk`

options.label: C
options.text: An SVI must be created first

options.label: D
options.text: The default route must be configured before connected routes appear

questions.question: Why does `ip ?` offer no `address` option on a switch interface?
questions.explanation: The interface is still in Layer 2 switchport mode. `no switchport` converts it to a routed port, after which an IP address can be assigned.

options.label: A
options.text: The switch does not support IP addressing

options.label: B
options.text: The interface is still a Layer 2 switchport — issue `no switchport` first

options.label: C
options.text: You must create the VLAN first

options.label: D
options.text: The interface is shut down

questions.question: PC2 can ping PC4 in the same VLAN but cannot ping its own default gateway. Where should you look first?
questions.explanation: Intra-VLAN traffic works, so the access ports, the VLAN and the Layer 2 path are fine. The problem is between the VLAN and its gateway — the router sub-interface, the SVI, or the trunk carrying that VLAN to the gateway.

options.label: A
options.text: PC2's IP address

options.label: B
options.text: PC4's VLAN assignment

options.label: C
options.text: The gateway side — the router sub-interface or SVI for that VLAN

options.label: D
options.text: The switch's MAC address table

questions.question: Which command shows whether a single port's administrative and operational mode is static access?
questions.explanation: `show interfaces <port> switchport` displays the administrative and operational mode of that specific port, along with its access VLAN and trunk settings.

options.label: A
options.text: show vlan brief

options.label: B
options.text: show interfaces fa0/3 switchport

options.label: C
options.text: show interfaces trunk

options.label: D
options.text: show ip interface brief

questions.question: In simulation mode the ping between two VLANs goes PC → SW2 → SW1 → destination and never reaches R1. Why?
questions.explanation: SW2 is a multilayer switch with SVIs for both VLANs, so it routes the packet internally from one SVI to the other. Only traffic leaving the LAN follows the default route to R1.

options.label: A
options.text: R1 is down

options.label: B
options.text: SW2 routed it internally between its VLAN SVIs

options.label: C
options.text: The trunk does not allow the VLAN toward R1

options.label: D
options.text: The packet was flooded rather than routed
